suggestions.rationale: Population-level evidence supports a modest association between hypothyroidism and clinical depression, but the effect is smaller than historically assumed and varies by thyroid phenotype and subgroup. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 studies involving 348,014 participants found an overall association, stronger for overt than subclinical hypothyroidism, with important sex-subgroup uncertainty. This mapping therefore supports association-focused research only; an individual's depressive disorder still requires chronology, thyroid-status, treatment-response, psychiatric-history, medication, sleep, pain, and psychosocial evaluation rather than automatic attribution to hypothyroidism.
evidenceGaps: Laboratory and endocrine documentation establishing overt or subclinical hypothyroidism and its chronology
Depressive-disorder diagnosis, symptom chronology, severity, and functional impact
Thyroid-treatment history and whether mood symptoms changed with biochemical correction
Medication, sleep, pain, substance-use, psychosocial, and other psychiatric contributors
Clinician assessment distinguishing population-level association from the individual's causal or aggravation theory

sourceReferences.citation: Bode H, Ivens B, Bschor T, Schwarzer G, Henssler J, Baethge C. Association of Hypothyroidism and Clinical Depression: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Psychiatry. 2021;78(12):1375-1383. PMID 34524390
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 25 studies and 348,014 participants found a modest overall association between hypothyroidism and clinical depression, stronger for overt than subclinical disease, with sensitivity and sex-subgroup uncertainty. Supports association-focused research rather than individual causal attribution.
